Name: pragmatic_implicature_gate
Title: Some Means Not All, In Some Languages: A Causal Study of a Language-Set Literal-vs-Implicated Interpretation Gate in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a shared, language-agnostic representation of an utterance's LITERAL meaning, but decide how strongly to enrich it with a PRAGMATIC implicature (e.g. 'some' -> 'not all'; an indirect request -> a command) via a language-conditioned 'implicature-strength' control. We deliberately state the mechanistic claim as a FAMILY of hypotheses of decreasing strength -- a single steerable direction, a low-rank subspace, or a distributed but localizable circuit -- so the contribution survives if the strict single-scalar version fails. Consequently the identical utterance is interpreted more literally in one language and more pragmatically in another; this gap scales with the query language's documented cross-linguistic implicature-rate (and typological distance) rather than resource level; and the control is separable from the literal-meaning computation. We soften 'literal meaning computed identically' to an operational criterion: cross-lingual transferability/invariance of a literal-meaning probe within a tolerance.
Related Work: Explicit novelty claims: (N1, problem) the query language covertly sets a literal-vs-pragmatic interpretation strength -- untested cross-lingually; (N2, finding) identical utterances get systematically different enrichment by language, tracking implicature typology not resource; (N3, mechanism) a separable, localizable implicature-strength control (direction/subspace/circuit) distinct from literal meaning; (N4, dataset) PRAG-GATE, a released multilingual literal-vs-implicated benchmark; (N5, safety) an indirect-phrasing compliance gap. Positioning against the closest mechanistic neighbors: multilingual refusal-direction work localizes a refusal gate but not a pragmatic-enrichment control and never addresses implicature; shared-concept-space work (Semantic Hub 2024; From Monolingual to Bilingual 2025) shows late-layer language decoding over shared content but not a language-set interpretation-strength step. What only our gate hypothesis explains: why the SAME literal content yields different enriched readings purely as a function of query language, with a steerable control. Existing multilingual pragmatics resources are behavioral and monolingual-scored (Harnessing the Linguistic Signal 2020; Pragmatic Inference of Scalar Implicature by LLMs 2024; Korean Indirect Speech Acts 2025; Partially Primed 2023; RSA, Goodman & Frank 2013) and lack matched cross-lingual literal-vs-enriched item pairs with the controls needed to answer the causal question -- which is why PRAG-GATE is required. Cross-linguistic pragmatics establishes divergent implicature rates and L1-to-L2 bias inheritance (Scalar Diversity and L2 Processing 2025). A non-obvious ALTERNATIVE theory we explicitly test against the gate account: the differences are language-specific instruction-following priors or translation artifacts, not a genuine interpretation-strength gate.
Abstract: When someone says 'some of the students passed', listeners often infer 'not all' - a scalar implicature. Languages differ measurably in how readily their speakers compute such enrichments, and L2 speakers inherit L1 pragmatic biases. We ask whether multilingual LLMs inherit language-specific pragmatics, and whether the query language covertly sets how literally versus pragmatically the model interprets an utterance. We hypothesize a shared, language-agnostic literal meaning enriched via a language-conditioned implicature-strength control, and -- to avoid over-committing -- frame the mechanism as a family of hypotheses (single direction, low-rank subspace, or localizable distributed circuit). We build and will RELEASE PRAG-GATE, a controlled set spanning scalar implicatures ('some','most','or','try'), indirect requests, and indirect answers/refusals, each rendered across 12+ languages with documented divergent implicature rates and paired with a question distinguishing the literal from the enriched interpretation, with a rigorous literal-vs-enriched annotation protocol (native-speaker labels, agreement thresholds, exclusion of ambiguous items) and translation controls (independent human translations, back-translation, language-internal paraphrases). Behaviorally we measure per-language implicature rate on identical utterances and test the gate account against two alternatives -- language-specific instruction-following priors and translation artifacts -- using translate-to-English/round-trip and monolingual paraphrase controls. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared literal-meaning representation transferable across languages within a tolerance, (ii) use activation patching, causal mediation, and subspace interventions (with random-direction sham and layerwise-robustness controls) to test that the literal meaning is shared while a separable enrichment control differs, and (iii) steer the control up/down without changing literal content. A safety subset (indirect harmful requests, indirect refusals) is evaluated with a specified refusal taxonomy and coarse scoring, measuring a cross-lingual indirect-phrasing compliance gap without overclaiming broad jailbreak impact. Either outcome is informative for multilingual evaluation, alignment, and deployment. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Dataset PRAG-GATE (constructed, to be released) in three pragmatic categories: (a) SCALAR ('some','most','or','might','try') with a follow-up question / NLI hypothesis distinguishing literal ('some' -> possibly all) from enriched ('some' -> not all); (b) INDIRECT REQUESTS ('Can you pass the salt?', 'It's cold in here'); (c) INDIRECT ANSWERS/REFUSALS ('Are you coming? -- I have to work'). ~150 base items/category with matched clearly-literal and clearly-direct controls; per-item literal-vs-enriched gold labels from native speakers with reported inter-annotator agreement and ambiguous-item exclusion. Rendered in 12+ languages with documented divergent implicature rates, 4+ families/scripts, via independent human translation + back-translation audit + language-internal paraphrases. Expected per-language implicature rates are grounded in cross-linguistic scalar-diversity data; a per-language implicature-typology distance and multiple resource proxies are pre-registered. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen, 3 paraphrase seeds. Controls throughout for language-ID effects, decoding/prompt-format, tokenization length, instruction-tuning distribution, and answer-matching artifacts; pooled/clause-final representations, tokenization statistics reported. Power: item counts set so a 20 pp cross-language rate gap and Spearman >=0.5 are detectable at 80% power; all metrics report bootstrap CIs.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- a language-set literal-vs-implicated gate, behavioral, vs alternatives): Decisive metric: per-language IMPLICATURE RATE on identical utterances and cross-language disagreement on the same item; literal/direct controls should agree across languages (gap <=5 pp). Alternative-theory tests: translate-to-English and round-trip conditions and monolingual paraphrase controls distinguish a genuine query-language interpretation gate from language-specific instruction-following priors or translation artifacts (if the effect disappears under round-trip/paraphrase matching, it is an artifact). Convincing result: cross-language implicature-rate gap on identical items >=20 pp while controls agree AND the gap survives the round-trip/paraphrase controls. Indecision band: 8-20 pp = weak; <8 pp, or gap removed by controls = no language-set gate / artifact, refuting H2.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the gap tracks implicature-typology, not resource): Predictors: pre-registered per-language implicature-typology distance vs multiple resource proxies. Decisive metric: Spearman(per-language implicature-rate deviation, typology) vs Spearman(deviation, resource), bootstrap CIs, mixed-effects across models; key contrast = a lower-resource high-rate language vs a higher-resource low-rate one. Convincing result: |Spearman with typology| >=0.5 and exceeds |Spearman with resource| by >=0.2; if the language count is too small for a robust correlation we report it as correlational and tone down causal language. Indecision band: within 0.05-0.2 = mixed; typology not stronger = refuted.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- shared literal meaning, causal late gate; multiple mechanistic tests): (a) train probes/logit-lens at each layer to decode the LITERAL truth-conditional content, test cross-lingual transfer (train one language, test others) -- the operational criterion for 'shared' is transfer within a tolerance (within 10 pp of in-language), NOT identity -- contrasted with a probe decoding the enriched reading; (b) activation-patch the mid-layer literal-meaning representation across runs; (c) causal MEDIATION analysis and SUBSPACE interventions on the late pragmatic-decision components, with layerwise-robustness checks and a random-direction sham control. Decisive metrics: literal-meaning probe cross-lingual transfer accuracy; rate at which patching the literal representation flips interpretation vs rate at which manipulating the late gate flips it, each above the sham. Convincing result: literal-meaning probe transfers within 10 pp of in-language while the enriched-reading probe varies by language; patching the literal representation flips interpretation in <=15% of cases while manipulating the late gate flips it in >=40%, above sham -- localizing the effect to a language-set gate; the mechanism is reported at whichever level of the hypothesis family (direction/subspace/circuit) the interventions support. Indecision band: late-gate flip 20-40% = partial; literal-probe transfer >25 pp below, literal-patch flipping >30%, or sham matching = literal meaning not shared, refuting H1.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- a locatable, steerable implicature-strength control, with a scoped safety demonstration): recover an implicature-strength direction/subspace (difference between enriched- and literal-reading runs pooled across languages); steer to (a) INDUCE enrichment in a low-rate language, (b) SUPPRESS it in a high-rate language, (c) dose-response. Systems compared: steering vs explicit prompting ('interpret pragmatically') vs translate-first vs matched-norm random-direction steer (sham). Safety subset: indirect harmful requests and indirect refusals from public red-team resources, scored with a specified refusal taxonomy (refuse / comply / partial) and coarse outputs; no novel operational content released; responsible disclosure. Decisive metrics (in order): induced/suppressed implicature rate; literal-content preservation (specificity, decoded literal meaning unchanged >=95%); fluency (perplexity); and, on the safety subset, the cross-lingual compliance gap on indirect harmful requests and its reduction when the gate is steered up. Convincing result: steering changes implicature rate by >=20 pp in the intended direction with literal content preserved and fluency unharmed, beats the sham, and steering the gate up raises refusal of implied harmful intent in under-enriching languages. Indecision band: 8-20 pp = partial; <8 pp, literal content altered (>5%), or sham matches = not a clean separable control, refuting H3. We frame the safety result as a scoped, coarse demonstration, not broad jailbreak generality.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of 'literal meaning' or 'implicature-strength' may reflect the readout basis; causal patching, mediation, and subspace interventions (Exp. 3) and steering (Exp. 4) with random-direction sham and layerwise-robustness controls, plus the literal-content specificity check, promote correlation to mechanism, and we report the mechanism only at the level (direction/subspace/circuit) the evidence supports. 2. Whether an utterance is 'enriched' is gradient and context-dependent; we restrict to high-agreement items with a rigorous native-speaker annotation protocol and clear literal/direct controls. 3. Cross-lingual differences might be genuine pragmatic-norm variation, language-specific instruction-following priors, or translation artifacts rather than a gate; the shared-literal-probe transfer, the literal-same/gate-differs patching, and the round-trip/paraphrase controls (Exp. 1) are designed to separate these. 4. The typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on language contrasts; we pre-register distance and multiple resource proxies, use mixed-effects modeling, and tone down causal language if the language count is small. 5. Strong models may compute implicatures faithfully per language, shrinking the effect; documenting faithful language-specific pragmatics is still positive, and the induction/suppression steering yields causal evidence. 6. The safety subset touches harmful topics; only borderline public red-team items, coarse refuse/comply scoring with a specified taxonomy, no novel operational content, responsible disclosure, and we avoid overclaiming broad jailbreak relevance from a small demonstration. 7. Tokenization differs across scripts; pooled/clause-final representations and reported tokenization statistics address this. 8. Steering may trade interpretation change for fluency/literal preservation; we report all three. 9. 'Computed identically' is operationalized as transferability/invariance within a tolerance, not literal identity. 10. Either outcome is informative for multilingual evaluation, alignment, and deployment; PRAG-GATE and analysis tools will be released. 11. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.
